photo.name: photographic print; stereoscope photograph
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); stereoscope photograph
photo.reason: The photo shows a domed wigwam dwelling with three Ho-Chunk (Winnebago) people wrapped in blankets peering inside, a documentary image of their traditional dwelling and dress. This directly matches the claimed ethnicity.

photo.name: photographic print; stereoscope photograph
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); stereoscope photograph
photo.reason: This is a documentary 19th-century photograph of a Winnebago (Ho-Chunk) chief and community gathered before a tipi with decorative panels, clothing, and other people, matching the claimed ethnicity's daily/ceremonial life.

photo.name: carte-de-visite
photo.title: carte-de-visite (black and white)
photo.reason: Carte-de-visite photograph of Winneshiek, a Winnebago (Ho-Chunk) chief, in full regalia with bear-claw necklace, bow and arrows, and pipe, photographed at Fort Snelling — a documentary portrait of Ho-Chunk dress and material culture.

photo.name: photographic print; stereoscope photograph
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); stereoscope photograph
photo.reason: Studio portrait of a Winnebago (Ho-Chunk) woman in traditional dress with shell jewelry, holding an infant in a decorated cradleboard—directly documenting the group's dress and material culture.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard; photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: Studio postcard portrait of Chief White Wing, a Ho-Chunk man from Wisconsin Dells, shown in full traditional regalia (feather headdress, bone breastplate, choker, beadwork) holding a pipe — a documentary photo of the people's dress and material culture.

photo.name: carte-de-visite
photo.title: carte-de-visite (black and white)
photo.reason: Studio carte-de-visite portrait of two Winnebago (Ho-Chunk) men in traditional dress—feathered headdress, beaded necklaces, leggings, moccasins, and a carved bow/blanket—documenting attire and material culture of the claimed people.

photo.name: photographic print; carte-de-visite
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); carte-de-visite
photo.reason: This is a studio carte-de-visite portrait of George Humphrey, identified as a "Winnebago" (Ho-Chunk) man wrapped in a blanket, matching the claimed ethnicity.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard; photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: The postcard shows Ho-Chunk women and children in traditional dress with woven baskets at a tent encampment set up at a county fair, documenting their dress and craft. This matches the claimed ethnicity as a documentary photo of Ho-Chunk people and their material culture.

photo.name: photographic print; stereoscope photograph
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); stereoscope photograph
photo.reason: A studio stereoscope portrait of a Winnebago (Ho-Chunk) woman and child in a painted-backdrop studio setting, wearing period dress and ornaments; this is a documentary photograph of the people themselves, matching the claimed ethnicity.

instruments.name: Whistle
instruments.title: Whistle
instruments.reason: The image shows a wooden whistle/flute-like instrument with sinew, ribbon, and metal thimble decoration, consistent with Ho-Chunk (Winnebago) craftsmanship as attributed in the museum record.

garment.name: Bag
garment.title: Bandolier Bag
garment.reason: This is a classic Great Lakes beaded bandolier bag with dense geometric beadwork, a well-known regalia item made by Ho-Chunk and related Woodlands peoples; the "(?)" simply flags normal attribution uncertainty within Great Lakes beadwork, not a named alternative culture.

masks-ritual.name: Bowl and bag
masks-ritual.title: Medicine Bundle Bowl and Bag
masks-ritual.reason: The image shows a carved wooden bowl (with duck-head handle) and a woven medicine bundle bag, both Ho-Chunk-made objects used in ritual/medicine practice; the museum's own materials description confirms wood and native-tanned skin, not ceramic.
